title: Brain injury activist Shane Christie diagnosed with ‘high-stage’ CTE after taking own life
content:
Former rugby union player and brain injury activist Shane Christie has been posthumously diagnosed with CTE after taking his own life in August 2025.

The New Zealander had played for the Maori All Blacks, Highlanders and Tasman Mako before retiring after repeated concussions in 2018. He died the day before his 40th birthday.

Christie’s former partner Holly Parkes told The Athletic that the news meant “his life was vindicated”, but that it was time “we listen and change”.

He initially became an activist after the death of his best friend and former teammate Billy Guyton in May 2023. Like Christie, Guyton also took his own life and was posthumously diagnosed with stage two CTE — scientists reported that the two hemispheres of his brains had become separated due to the blows he had sustained.

Christie’s brain was subsequently examined by a pathologist at the country’s National Brain Bank. He had spoken publicly about the belief he was suffering from CTE.

“As I now understand the effects that concussion had on Billy’s brain and witnessing the drastic changes in his life, I can only assume that I’ve developed CTE myself,” Christie wrote in the months before his death.

The Athletic reported on Christie and Guyton’s deaths last September, with both players’ families alleging, in testimonies supported by Christie’s own writings, that they had been left without significant medical or financial support from rugby’s governing bodies in the final years of their life, despite remaining employees.

Speaking at a hearing regarding the release of Christie’s autopsy, Coroner Ian Telford stated: “Note is made of the fact that (Shane) was a professional rugby player who had suffered several significant concussions during the course of his playing career.

“In accordance with his wishes, and with the consent of the next of kin, his brain was donated to the National Brain Bank, University of Auckland, for detailed examination by Dr Clinton Turner a pathologist at LabPLUS, Auckland Hospital.

“In summary Dr Turner confirms the diagnosis of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) which he characterises as ‘high stage’. He also noted, incidentally, the development of early age-related changes.”

Christie and Guyton’s families told The Athletic in September that they wanted NZ Rugby and the New Zealand Rugby Players Association (NZRPA) to mirror the NFL by recognising a causal relationship between head knocks and CTE, which they say would allow them to better support players.

NZ Rugby told The Athletic in a statement that they recognised an association between the two, but that “not enough research using study designs that would support causal statements has been done yet”.

“Bill and Shane weren’t listened to when they were alive,” said Christie’s former partner Holly Parkes after the diagnosis. “They were put through a course of misdiagnosis and mistreatment by people who chose not to consider that their brains were damaged by the sport they loved.

“No one paid any attention to Shane when he stood up and shouted that there was something biologically, not psychologically, wrong with his brain. Now he’s dead and thanks to his last act of giving, donating his brain, his life is vindicated. He died with CTE, a serious brain disease, and it’s time we listen and change.

“Shane’s final game of rugby was for the Maori All Blacks in 2016. Three players from that game have now died in the same way. Does that not seem insane?”
